claims.source: The regions of the genome coding for these molecules are composed of highly repetitive sequences, with hundreds to thousands of members of each family, as well as substantial numbers of transposable elements, microsatellite, and tandem repeats (Talavera-López et al., 2021; El-Sayed et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Talavera-López et al., 2021; El-Sayed et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2021

claims.claim: Both preponderate clonal evolution and sexual reproduction have been proposed for T. cruzi.
claims.source: The reproductive mode of these parasitic protozoans has been widely debated, and both preponderate clonal evolution (Tibayrenc and Ayala, 2012; Tibayrenc and Ayala, 2013) and sexual reproduction (Ramírez and Llewellyn, 2014; Schwabl et al., 2019; Inbar et al., 2019) have been proposed.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Tibayrenc and Ayala, 2012; Tibayrenc and Ayala, 2013 for clonal evolution and Ramírez and Llewellyn, 2014; Schwabl et al., 2019; Inbar et al., 2019 for sexual reproduction

claims.claim: Many eukaryotic pathogens have essentially clonal population structures while also having non-obligate sexual cycles.
claims.source: Many eukaryotic pathogens have essentially clonal population structures while also having non-obligate sexual cycles, which may enable them to adapt to environmental changes (Heitman, 2006; Lewis et al., 2011; Steensels et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Heitman, 2006; Lewis et al., 2011; Steensels et al., 2021

claims.claim: The most well-studied mating system in trypanosomatids is that of Trypanosoma brucei.
claims.source: In trypanosomatids, the most well-studied mating system is that of Trypanosoma brucei, for which a meiotic process is well supported based on the identification of a haploid parasite stage in the vector (Peacock et al., 2014) and on the patterns of allele inheritance and recombination observed in experimental hybrids (MacLeod et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Peacock et al., 2014 and MacLeod et al., 2005

claims.claim: Six distinct genetic clades of T. cruzi have been recognized, named TcI to TcVI.
claims.source: In T. cruzi, great genetic and phenotypic diversity is observed, and six distinct genetic clades have been recognized, named TcI to TcVI (discrete typing units or DTU-I to -VI) (Zingales et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Zingales et al., 2012

claims.claim: TcV and TcVI are recent, natural inter-lineage hybrids of TcII and TcIII.
claims.source: Genotyping analysis indicates that TcV and TcVI are recent, natural inter-lineage hybrids of TcII and TcIII, showing that recombination events have shaped the evolution of T. cruzi lineages (Schwabl et al., 2019; Lewis et al., 2011; Messenger and Miles, 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Schwabl et al., 2019; Lewis et al., 2011; Messenger and Miles, 2015

claims.claim: The formation of T. cruzi hybrids in vitro has been described.
claims.source: In addition to natural evidence of hybridization, the formation of T. cruzi hybrids in vitro was also described (Gaunt et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Gaunt et al., 2003

claims.claim: Genetic marker analyses of hybrid strains showed multi-allelic (non-Mendelian) inheritance of microsatellite alleles and an elevated DNA content.
claims.source: Genetic marker analyses of hybrid strains showed multi-allelic (non-Mendelian) inheritance of microsatellite alleles and an elevated DNA content (Gaunt et al., 2003; Lewis et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Gaunt et al., 2003; Lewis et al., 2009

claims.claim: The hybridization events in T. cruzi were proposed to occur via a parasexual mechanism, similar to those observed in certain fungi.
claims.source: The hybridization events in T. cruzi were proposed to occur via a parasexual mechanism, similar to those observed in certain fungi (Lewis et al., 2011; Steensels et al., 2021; Gaunt et al., 2003; Bennett, 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Lewis et al., 2011; Steensels et al., 2021; Gaunt et al., 2003; Bennett, 2015

claims.claim: Two closely related TcI strains (P1, P2) and three hybrid clones (1C2, 1D12, 2C1) were selected for the study.
claims.source: To investigate the effects of clonal reproduction and genetic exchange on the T. cruzi genome at the microevolutionary scale, we selected two closely related TcI strains (P1, P2) and three hybrid clones that were generated from a P1 × P2 cross (1C2, 1D12, 2C1) (Gaunt et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: Describes the experimental design and materials used in the study

claims.claim: The two parents and three hybrids were continuously cultured as epimastigote forms for 5 years, equivalent to approximately 800 generations.
claims.source: The two parents and three hybrids were included in an in vitro evolution experiment in which they were continuously cultured as epimastigote forms for 5 years, equivalent to approximately 800 generations of replication by binary fission (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: Describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1A

claims.claim: The DNA content of the two parental lines remained approximately constant during the microevolution experiment.
claims.source: We observed that the DNA content of the two parental lines remained approximately constant (Figure 1B–D).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B-D

claims.claim: At the start of the experiment, the total DNA content of the hybrid clones was approximately 70% greater than the parentals.
claims.source: At the start of the experiment, the total DNA content of the hybrid clones was approximately 70% greater than the parentals (Figure 1C, D, Lewis et al., 2009), which equated to slightly below expectations for a tetraploid parasite with one kinetoplast (containing mitochondrial DNA), that is, a 4n1k (4C) genome size.
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C, D and citation to Lewis et al., 2009

claims.claim: The DNA content of the hybrids became progressively lower over time, up to a maximum decrease of 22.5% by generation 800.
claims.source: Over the course of the microevolution experiment, in contrast to P1 and P2, we found that the DNA content of the hybrids became progressively lower over time, up to a maximum decrease of 22.5% by generation 800.
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry measurements over time

claims.claim: Genome erosion in the hybrids occurred at an average rate of 23 kb per generation.
claims.source: By extrapolation from the estimated genome sizes of P1 (94.5 Mb) and P2 (92.5 Mb) (Lewis et al., 2009), these data indicate genome erosion in the hybrids occurred at an average rate of 23 kb per generation.
claims.evidence: Calculated from flow cytometry data and genome size estimates from Lewis et al., 2009

claims.claim: Hybrid 2C1 showed gradual genome erosion at each time point, with all three 800 generation evolved clones approximating a 3C genome size.
claims.source: Hybrid 2C1 showed gradual genome erosion at each time point, with all three 800 generation evolved clones approximating a 3C genome size.
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data over time

claims.claim: Hybrid 1C2 showed a more intermittent pattern of genome erosion, with most erosion occurring between 0–200 and 400–600 generations.
claims.source: Hybrid 1C2 showed a more intermittent pattern – most of the erosion occurred between 0–200 and 400–600 generations, reaching a 3C genome size, but interestingly, 2 of the 800 generation clones gained ~10% more DNA than at t=600.
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data over time

claims.claim: Hybrid 1D12 had an initial 9% loss between t=0 and t=200, but was then quite stable over time between 3C and 4C.
claims.source: Lastly, hybrid 1D12 had an initial 9% loss between t=0 and t=200, but was then quite stable over time between 3C and 4C.
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data over time

claims.claim: Three of the nine evolved hybrid clones had lost at least one microsatellite allele.
claims.source: We found that three of the nine evolved hybrid clones had lost at least one microsatellite allele (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by microsatellite genotyping data in Supplementary file 1

claims.claim: The haploid estimated genome size of P1 differed from P2 by approximately 2 Mbp.
claims.source: The haploid estimated genome size of P1 differed from P2 by approximately 2 Mbp, and both parental strains genomes were found to be slightly larger than the 44 Mbp reference TcI-Sylvio X10/1 strain (Talavera-López et al., 2021), in line with flow cytometry-based DNA content measurements (Lewis et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by genome assembly data and citations to Talavera-López et al., 2021 and Lewis et al., 2009

claims.claim: The genome-wide average SNP density was 9.28 and 3.71 SNP/kb for P1 and P2, respectively.
claims.source: The resultant genome-wide average SNP density was 9.28 and 3.71 SNP/kb for P1 and P2, respectively (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by SNP calling data shown in Table 1

claims.claim: Most SNPs were located within repetitive regions, particularly in areas containing surface molecule gene family members.
claims.source: Most SNPs were located within repetitive regions, particularly in areas containing surface molecule gene family members, which can be related to gene expansion in these regions.
claims.evidence: Inferred from SNP distribution analysis

claims.claim: P1 displays tandem-repeated and surface molecule-coding regions expanded in comparison to P2.
claims.source: Indeed, copy number variation (CNV) analysis showed that P1 displays these tandem-repeated and surface molecule-coding regions expanded in comparison to P2.
claims.evidence: Supported by CNV analysis data

claims.claim: SNP density in high-quality mapping regions was 2.84 and 2.11 SNPs/kb for P1 and P2, respectively.
claims.source: SNP density in the retained high-quality regions was 2.84 and 2.11 SNPs/kb for P1 and P2, respectively (Table 1), and a total of 68,616 and 34,843 SNPs exclusive for each parental strain were catalogued for use in the analysis of the hybrid strains (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: Supported by SNP calling data shown in Table 1 and Figure 1E

claims.claim: The average SNP density in high-quality mapping regions was higher in all hybrids than in parental strains.
claims.source: The average SNP density in these regions was higher in all hybrids than in parental strains: 3.48 SNP/kb for 1C2-0, 3.29 SNP/kb for 1D12-0, and 3.49 SNP/kb for 2C1-0 (Table 1), partially due to the presence of alleles from both parental strains.
claims.evidence: Supported by SNP calling data shown in Table 1

claims.claim: Additional SNPs common to all hybrids and SNPs exclusive to each hybrid clone were identified in both coding and non-coding regions.
claims.source: In addition to the SNPs clearly inherited from each parental strain, additional SNPs common to all hybrids and SNPs exclusive to each hybrid clone were identified in both coding and non-coding regions, revealing sample-specific patterns (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: Supported by SNP analysis data shown in Figure 1E

claims.claim: De novo mutations common to all hybrids and exclusive to each hybrid clone were predicted to generate a higher percentage of non-synonymous changes compared to mutations inherited from the parental strains.
claims.source: Interestingly, de novo mutations common to all hybrids and exclusive to each hybrid clone were predicted to generate a higher percentage of non-synonymous changes in comparison to the mutations inherited from the parental strains (Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by SNP effect prediction data in Supplementary file 3

claims.claim: The ratio of non-synonymous changes per synonymous changes was higher in de novo mutations than in those inherited from the parental strains.
claims.source: Indeed, the ratio of non-synonymous changes per synonymous changes was higher in the de novo mutations common to all hybrids (2.36 for 1C2-0, 2.25 for 1D12-0, and 2.19 for 2C1-0), and exclusive to each hybrid clone (2.40 for 1C2-0, 2.23 for 1D12-0, and 2.37 for 2C1-0) than in those inherited from the parental strains (1.41 for 1C2-0, 1.40 for 1D12-0, and 1.42 for 2C1-0) (Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by SNP effect prediction data in Supplementary file 3

claims.claim: The ratio of surface protein-coding genes per non-surface protein-coding genes is approximately 4-fold higher in SNPs common to all hybrids and in SNPs exclusive to each hybrid clone than in those inherited from the parental strains.
claims.source: This ratio is approximately 4-fold higher in SNPs common to all hybrids and in SNPs exclusive to each hybrid clone than in those inherited from the parental strains (Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: Supported by SNP distribution analysis in Supplementary file 4

claims.claim: The ratio of non-synonymous mutations in surface protein-coding genes per non-synonymous mutations in other genes was approximately 3.3-fold higher in the hybrid clone-specific SNPs compared to those inherited from the parental strains.
claims.source: Interestingly, this ratio was approximately 3.3-fold higher in the hybrid clone-specific SNPs in comparison to those inherited from the parental strains (Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: Supported by SNP distribution analysis in Supplementary file 5

claims.claim: Aneuploidy was observed in the P2 strain, involving trisomy of chromosomes 2 and 21.
claims.source: Aneuploidy was observed in the P2 strain, involving trisomy of chromosomes 2 and 21 (Figure 2A, B).
claims.evidence: Supported by RDC and AB analysis shown in Figure 2A, B

claims.claim: The RDC analysis indicated aneuploidy in chromosome 44 in the P1 strain.
claims.source: The RDC analysis indicated aneuploidy in chromosome 44 in the P1 strain, but due to the lack of regions with high-quality SNPs, it was not possible to confirm this in the AB analysis (Figure 2A, B).
claims.evidence: Supported by RDC analysis shown in Figure 2A, B, but not confirmed by AB analysis

claims.claim: In both parental strains, a peak at 50% was observed in allele balance analysis, while in the hybrids, peaks at 25% and 75% or 50% were observed.
claims.source: In both parental strains, a peak at 50% was observed, while in the hybrids, peaks at 25% and 75% or 50% were observed (Figure 2C), which is expected for diploid and tetraploid genomes, respectively (Reis-Cunha and Bartholomeu, 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by allele balance analysis shown in Figure 2C and citation to Reis-Cunha and Bartholomeu, 2019

claims.claim: The hybrids displayed ~70% greater DNA content than the parental strains based on flow cytometry.
claims.source: This ploidy estimation is in accordance with the previous DNA content estimation based on flow cytometry data, in which the hybrids displayed ~70% greater DNA content than the parental strains (Figure 1C, Lewis et al., 2009), given that this method could not determine the relative amounts of mitochondrial kDNA and nuclear DNA.
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C and citation to Lewis et al., 2009

claims.claim: Inheritance of SNPs exclusive to both parental strains were observed in the hybrid genomes.
claims.source: Inheritance of SNPs exclusive to both parental strains were observed in the hybrid genomes (Figure 1E), which shows that the tetrasomic profile observed resulted from a contribution from both parental chromosomes.
claims.evidence: Supported by SNP inheritance analysis shown in Figure 1E

claims.claim: The trisomies in chromosomes 2 and 21 of P2 were no longer observed in any replicate clone after growth in culture.
claims.source: The trisomies in chromosomes 2 and 21 of P2 (Figure 2A) were no longer observed in any replicate clone after growth in culture (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Supported by CCNV analysis shown in Figure 2A and Figure 4A

claims.claim: New aneuploidies were identified in the parental strains after culture growth, involving trisomy of chromosomes 37 and 45 in all P1 clones and trisomy of chromosomes 32 and 37 in all P2 clones.
claims.source: New aneuploidies were identified in the parental strains, involving trisomy of chromosomes 37 and 45 in all P1 clones and trisomy of chromosomes 32 and 37 in all P2 clones (Figure 4A, B).
claims.evidence: Supported by CCNV analysis shown in Figure 4A, B

claims.claim: Hybrid 2C1 displayed a clear transition from a tetraploid to a triploid pattern after growth in culture.
claims.source: Indeed, hybrid 2C1 displayed a clear transition from a tetraploid to a triploid pattern after growth in culture (Figure 4C), suggesting that genome erosion eventually leads to a return towards diploidy after the hybridization event, as observed in the naturally occurring TcV and TcVI hybrids (Lewis et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by ploidy estimation shown in Figure 4C and citation to Lewis et al., 2009

claims.claim: Tetrasomic profiles in chromosomes 19 and 37 were present in all hybrid clones after culture growth.
claims.source: Despite the patterns of genome erosion, tetrasomic profiles in chromosomes 19 and 37 were present in all hybrid clones after culture growth (Figure 4A, B).
claims.evidence: Supported by CCNV analysis shown in Figure 4A, B

claims.claim: The genome erosion seems to be gradual phenomena, with sequential losses of chromosome copies and regions rather than coordinated jumps between ploidy levels.
claims.source: Taken together with previous DNA content analysis of intermediate time points (Figure 1), our results from the different in vitro evolved clones indicate that the genome erosion seems to be gradual phenomena, with sequential losses of chromosome copies and regions rather than coordinated jumps between ploidy levels.
claims.evidence: Inferred from flow cytometry and CCNV data over time shown in Figure 1

claims.claim: Similar gene categories showed CNV in both parental and hybrid clones after culture growth.
claims.source: Despite the stability of DNA content in parental clones during our experiment (Figure 1C, D), similar gene categories showed CNV in both parental and hybrid clones after culture growth (Supplementary files 6–12).
claims.evidence: Supported by CNV analysis data in Supplementary files 6-12

claims.claim: Gene losses occurred mainly in host-parasite interaction genes such as surface protein-coding genes and genes related to exocytosis and cell secretion.
claims.source: Gene losses occurred mainly in host-parasite interaction genes such as surface protein-coding genes and genes related to exocytosis and cell secretion, while genes related to macromolecule metabolism, ion transport, and cell division showed an increase in copy numbers (Figure 6; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by CNV analysis shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: Genes related to macromolecule metabolism, ion transport, and cell division showed an increase in copy numbers after culture growth.
claims.source: Gene losses occurred mainly in host-parasite interaction genes such as surface protein-coding genes and genes related to exocytosis and cell secretion, while genes related to macromolecule metabolism, ion transport, and cell division showed an increase in copy numbers (Figure 6; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by CNV analysis shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: Chromosomes 19 and 37 remained tetrasomic in all hybrid clones after culture growth.
claims.source: Despite the events of genome erosion, chromosomes 19 and 37 remained tetrasomic in all hybrid clones and an extra copy of chromosome 37 is observed in all parental clones after culture growth (Figure 4B and Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: Supported by CCNV analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 5B

claims.claim: Chromosomes 19 and 37 contain long core regions with abundant housekeeping genes involved in cellular metabolism, DNA replication and transcription.
claims.source: Chromosomes 19 and 37 contain long core regions with abundant housekeeping genes involved in cellular metabolism, DNA replication and transcription (Supplementary files 10 and 11) which may contribute to fitness in culture.
claims.evidence: Supported by gene content analysis in Supplementary files 10 and 11

claims.claim: All P1 replicates showed a similar SNP density in the retained high-quality regions after culture growth.
claims.source: Regarding the parental strains, all P1 replicates showed a similar SNP density in the retained high-quality regions after culture growth (P1-0: 2.84; P1-1: 2.80; P1-2: 2.77; P1-3: 2.82), while all P2 replicates showed an increase in SNP density after culture growth (P2-0: 2.11; P2-1 2.78; P2-2 2.81; P2-3 2.66, Mann-Whitney, p=0.042) (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: Supported by SNP density analysis shown in Figure 7A with statistical test

claims.claim: All P2 replicates showed an increase in SNP density after culture growth.
claims.source: Regarding the parental strains, all P1 replicates showed a similar SNP density in the retained high-quality regions after culture growth (P1-0: 2.84; P1-1: 2.80; P1-2: 2.77; P1-3: 2.82), while all P2 replicates showed an increase in SNP density after culture growth (P2-0: 2.11; P2-1 2.78; P2-2 2.81; P2-3 2.66, Mann-Whitney, p=0.042) (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: Supported by SNP density analysis shown in Figure 7A with statistical test

claims.claim: The P2 replicates have a reduction in copies of HUS1-like encoding genes after culture growth.
claims.source: The P2 replicates have a reduction in copies of HUS1-like encoding genes, which are involved in DNA repair, after culture growth (Supplementary file 12).
claims.evidence: Supported by CNV analysis in Supplementary file 12

claims.claim: Many HUS1-like genes were located on chromosome 2.
claims.source: Our gene enrichment analysis showed that a number of these genes were located on chromosome 2 (Supplementary file 12), suggesting that the loss of trisomy in this chromosome could possibly have contributed to the higher number of mutations that was found in the P2 clones.
claims.evidence: Supported by gene enrichment analysis in Supplementary file 12

claims.claim: All evolved hybrid replicate clones, with exception of 1D12-3, showed a slight decrease in SNP density.
claims.source: All evolved hybrid replicate clones, with exception of 1D12-3, showed a slight decrease in SNP density (1C2-0: 3.48; 1C2-1: 2.96; 1C2-2: 3.26; 1C2-3: 3.10; 1D12-0: 3.29; 1D12-1: 3.24; 1D12-2: 3.22; 1D12-3: 3.36; 2C1-0: 3.49; 2C1-1: 3.34; 2C1-2: 2.64; 2C1-3: 3.25, Figure 7A), likely caused by the loss of genetic material.
claims.evidence: Supported by SNP density analysis shown in Figure 7A

claims.claim: Multiple new genomic variants were found in the in vitro evolved hybrid progeny, displaying patterns specific to each clonal isolate.
claims.source: Multiple new genomic variants were found in the in vitro evolved hybrid progeny, displaying patterns specific to each clonal isolate (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: Supported by SNP analysis shown in Figure 7A

claims.claim: The SNP density pattern per chromosome remained similar for all samples in first generation (t=0) and after culture growth (t=800).
claims.source: The SNP density pattern per chromosome remained similar for all samples in first generation (t=0) and after culture growth (t=800).
claims.evidence: Inferred from chromosome-level SNP density analysis

claims.claim: Some chromosomes (e.g. chromosomes 5, 11, 24, and 37) display higher SNP density than the others across all samples.
claims.source: Some chromosomes (e.g. chromosomes 5, 11, 24, and 37) display higher SNP density than the others across all samples (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: Supported by chromosome-level SNP density analysis shown in Figure 7B

claims.claim: P2 evolved clone replicates had an increase in SNP density in nearly all chromosomes.
claims.source: P2 evolved clone replicates had an increase in SNP density in nearly all chromosomes (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: Supported by chromosome-level SNP density analysis shown in Figure 7B

claims.claim: The emergence of novel SNPs after culture growth resulted in most of the non-synonymous mutations.
claims.source: The emergence of novel SNPs after culture growth resulted in most of the non-synonymous mutations.
claims.evidence: Inferred from SNP effect prediction analysis

claims.claim: The regions of the genome with higher genetic variation in all clone isolates contain surface protein-coding sequences.
claims.source: Interestingly, the regions of the genome with higher genetic variation in all clone isolates contain surface protein-coding sequences (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: Supported by SNP distribution analysis shown in Figure 7C

claims.claim: The ratio of non-synonymous mutations in surface protein-coding genes to non-synonymous mutations in other genes was higher for the mutations that appeared in each evolved parental clone compared to those present in the first generation.
claims.source: This ratio was higher for the mutations that appeared in each evolved parental clone in comparison to those present in the first generation (approx. 2.5-fold higher for P1 clones and 3.5-fold higher for P2 clones; Supplementary file 13).
claims.evidence: Supported by SNP distribution analysis in Supplementary file 13

claims.claim: A similar ratio of non-synonymous mutations in surface protein-coding genes to other genes was observed in the SNPs that appeared in each evolved hybrid clone and those exclusive to each hybrid clone present in the first generation.
claims.source: Regarding the hybrid strains, a similar ratio was observed in the SNPs that appeared in each evolved hybrid clone and those exclusive to each hybrid clone present in the first generation (Supplementary file 13).
claims.evidence: Supported by SNP distribution analysis in Supplementary file 13

claims.claim: Surface molecule-coding regions may mutate faster than the rest of the genome either by clonal or parasexual mechanisms.
claims.source: These results indicate that surface molecule-coding regions may mutate faster than the rest of the genome either by clonal or parasexual mechanisms, representing an important region of genomic diversification.
claims.evidence: Inferred from SNP distribution and mutation rate analysis

claims.claim: All initial hybrid clones were essentially tetraploid.
claims.source: The results from whole genome sequencing analysis of this T. cruzi genetic cross have clearly demonstrated that, while the parental strains were diploid, all initial hybrid clones were essentially tetraploid.
claims.evidence: Supported by ploidy estimation from allele balance and flow cytometry data

claims.claim: Genomic variants exclusive to both parental strains were present in all hybrid clones, indicating that the tetraploid profile resulted from the fusion of the two disomic parental genomes.
claims.source: We showed that genomic variants exclusive to both parental strains were present in all hybrid clones, indicating that the tetraploid profile observed is obtained by the fusion of the two disomic parental genomes, although more complex pathways cannot be ruled out in the absence of direct observational evidence.
claims.evidence: Inferred from SNP inheritance patterns

claims.claim: Genome erosion seems to be gradual, with sequential losses of chromosome copies rather than coordinated jumps between ploidy levels.
claims.source: In addition, we showed that genome erosion seems to be gradual, with sequential losses of chromosome copies rather than coordinated jumps between ploidy levels, though with some variation in erosion rates between different evolved hybrid lines.
claims.evidence: Inferred from flow cytometry and CCNV data over time

claims.claim: Hybridization in T. cruzi happened via a parasexual mechanism rather than a canonical meiotic process.
claims.source: As previously proposed (Lewis et al., 2011; Gaunt et al., 2003), our results confirmed that hybridization in T. cruzi happened via a parasexual mechanism rather than a canonical meiotic process.
claims.evidence: Supported by ploidy and inheritance data, with citations to Lewis et al., 2011; Gaunt et al., 2003

claims.claim: The hybridization phenomenon in T. cruzi resembles the parasexual cycle of the pathogenic fungus Candida albicans.
claims.source: This phenomenon resembles the parasexual cycle of the pathogenic fungus Candida albicans, which also involves diploid fusion followed by non-meiotic genome reduction back to aneuploids and diploids (reviewed by Bennett, 2015).
claims.evidence: Comparison to known mechanism in C. albicans, supported by citation to Bennett, 2015

claims.claim: Hybridization in T. brucei and possibly in Leishmania spp. has been associated with parental strains having undergone a meiosis-like process followed by a fusion of haploid cells.
claims.source: In contrast, hybridization in T. brucei and possibly in Leishmania spp. has been associated with parental strains having undergone a meiosis-like process followed by a fusion of haploid cells (Inbar et al., 2019; Peacock et al., 2014; Gibson et al., 2008; Rogers et al., 2014; Louradour et al., 2020; Van den Broeck et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Inbar et al., 2019; Peacock et al., 2014; Gibson et al., 2008; Rogers et al., 2014; Louradour et al., 2020; Van den Broeck et al., 2020

claims.claim: T. cruzi genomes are highly responsive to the environmental conditions.
claims.source: Our microevolution experiment has shown that T. cruzi genomes are highly responsive to the environmental conditions.
claims.evidence: Inferred from CNV and CCNV changes observed during culture growth

claims.claim: While surface gene numbers were being eroded after culture growth, genes involved in cell metabolism, cell division, and ion transport were being expanded.
claims.source: The CNV analysis showed that while surface gene numbers were being eroded after culture growth, genes involved in cell metabolism, cell division, and ion transport were being expanded.
claims.evidence: Supported by CNV analysis data

claims.claim: Aneuploidies have been widely reported in natural T. cruzi populations.
claims.source: Indeed, aneuploidies have been widely reported in natural T. cruzi populations, and although CCNV varies among and within DTUs, it seems constant within a given population (Schwabl et al., 2019; Reis-Cunha et al., 2015; Reis-Cunha et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Schwabl et al., 2019; Reis-Cunha et al., 2015; Reis-Cunha et al., 2018

claims.claim: In trypanosomatids, aneuploidy represents an important mechanism for rapidly overcoming environmental diversity.
claims.source: While in many multicellular organisms, aneuploidy is known to have severe consequences, in trypanosomatids it represents an important mechanism for rapidly overcoming environmental diversity (Reis-Cunha et al., 2018; Prieto Barja et al., 2017; Bussotti et al., 2018; Grünebast and Clos, 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Reis-Cunha et al., 2018; Prieto Barja et al., 2017; Bussotti et al., 2018; Grünebast and Clos, 2020

claims.claim: Aneuploidy is reversed quickly once the benefits of an extra chromosome expire.
claims.source: Aneuploidy is reversed quickly once the benefits of an extra chromosome expire, as observed in P2 aneuploidies in chromosomes 2 and 21.
claims.evidence: Inferred from observation of aneuploidy loss in P2 after culture growth

claims.claim: Trypanosomatids may control overexpression caused by additional gene copies at the protein level.
claims.source: In addition, trypanosomatids may control overexpression caused by additional gene copies, at the protein level (Dumetz, 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Dumetz, 2017

claims.claim: Aneuploidy in chromosome 37 was found in all parental and hybrid clones after culture growth, suggesting a benefit to parasite fitness in culture.
claims.source: We found aneuploidy in chromosome 37 in all parental and hybrid clones after culture growth, suggesting a benefit to parasite fitness in culture.
claims.evidence: Inferred from consistent observation of chromosome 37 aneuploidy across all clones

claims.claim: In Leishmania spp., the fixation of genetic alterations is the result of positive selection processes that adapt parasite fitness to a given ecology or transmission cycle.
claims.source: As observed in Leishmania spp., the fixation of genetic alterations is the result of positive selection processes that adapt parasite fitness to a given ecology or transmission cycle (Bussotti et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Bussotti et al., 2018

claims.claim: An increase in genetic sequence diversity was present after hybridization.
claims.source: Genome variant analyses showed that an increase in genetic sequence diversity was present after hybridization.
claims.evidence: Supported by SNP density analysis

claims.claim: Hybridization events are associated with a burst of novel mutations and a myriad of genomic rearrangements in distinct eukaryotes.
claims.source: Hybridization events are associated with a burst of novel mutations and a myriad of genomic rearrangements (e.g. transpositions, genome size changes, chromosomal rearrangements) in distinct eukaryotes (Steensels et al., 2021; Samarasinghe et al., 2020).

results.result: A microevolution experiment was conducted with two TcI parental strains (P1, P2) and three hybrid clones (1C2, 1D12, 2C1) cultured for ~800 generations. Parental DNA content remained stable while hybrid DNA content decreased progressively by up to 22.5%, corresponding to genome erosion at ~23 kb/generation, with variable patterns among hybrid lines.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C26 provide converging evidence from flow cytometry measurements over time showing stable parental DNA content and progressive hybrid genome erosion. The experimental design is clearly described (C18-C19), measurements are quantitative (C20-C23), and line-specific patterns are documented (C24-C26). The erosion rate calculation (C23) is appropriately derived from flow cytometry data and published genome size estimates.

results.result: Three of nine evolved hybrid clones lost at least one microsatellite allele during culture growth.
results.evaluation: Claim C27 is supported by microsatellite genotyping data presented in Supplementary file 1. This provides independent molecular evidence for genome instability in hybrids, complementing the flow cytometry data.

results.result: Parental strains P1 and P2 differ in genome size (~2 Mbp) and SNP density (9.28 vs 3.71 SNP/kb genome-wide; 2.84 vs 2.11 SNP/kb in high-quality regions). P1 shows expansion of tandem-repeated and surface molecule-coding regions compared to P2.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C32 are supported by genome assembly data and SNP calling analysis with appropriate quality filtering. The characterization of parental genome differences provides essential baseline data for interpreting hybrid genomes. CNV analysis (C31) supports the observed SNP distribution patterns.

results.result: Hybrid strains show increased SNP density (3.29-3.49 SNP/kb) compared to parents, with additional de novo mutations enriched for non-synonymous changes (NS/S ratio ~2.2-2.4 vs ~1.4 in inherited SNPs) and disproportionately affecting surface protein-coding genes (~4-fold enrichment).
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C38 demonstrate increased genetic diversity in hybrids with quantitative support from SNP density analysis (C33), identification of de novo mutations (C34-C35), and effect prediction showing elevated NS/S ratios (C36) and surface gene enrichment (C37-C38). The data consistently support a burst of mutations associated with hybridization.

results.result: Parental strains are diploid (allele balance peaks at 50%) while initial hybrid clones are tetraploid (peaks at 25%/75% or 50%), with ~70% greater DNA content. P2 shows trisomy of chromosomes 2 and 21. Hybrids inherit SNPs from both parents, indicating tetraploidy results from fusion of diploid parental genomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C43 provide converging evidence for ploidy from multiple methods: read depth coverage (RDC), allele balance (AB) analysis, and flow cytometry. The combination of methods strengthens the conclusion. However, C40 notes that chromosome 44 aneuploidy in P1 could not be confirmed by AB analysis due to lack of high-quality SNPs, appropriately acknowledging a limitation.

results.result: After 800 generations, parental aneuploidies changed (P2 lost trisomies in chr 2/21; both parents gained trisomy in chr 37). Hybrid 2C1 transitioned from tetraploid to triploid. Chromosomes 19 and 37 remained tetrasomic in all hybrids. Genome erosion appears gradual with sequential losses rather than coordinated ploidy jumps.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C48 are supported by CCNV analysis at generation 800 combined with intermediate time point flow cytometry data. The observation of dynamic aneuploidy and gradual erosion is well-documented. The retention of tetrasomy in specific chromosomes (C47) is consistently observed across all hybrid clones.

results.result: Despite stable parental DNA content, both parental and hybrid clones showed CNV after culture growth. Gene losses occurred mainly in surface protein-coding and host-parasite interaction genes, while genes for metabolism, ion transport, and cell division increased. Chromosomes 19 and 37 (enriched in housekeeping genes) remained tetrasomic in hybrids.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C53 are supported by CNV analysis data in Supplementary files 6-12 and gene content analysis. The functional categorization of genes showing gains vs losses is biologically coherent and consistent with adaptation to culture conditions. The retention of housekeeping gene-rich chromosomes (C52-C53) provides a plausible fitness explanation.

results.result: P1 clones maintained stable SNP density after culture growth while P2 clones showed significant increase (2.11 to 2.66-2.81 SNP/kb, p=0.042). P2 clones lost copies of HUS1-like DNA repair genes, many located on chromosome 2, potentially explaining the increased mutation rate.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C57 are supported by SNP density analysis with appropriate statistical testing (Mann-Whitney test) and CNV analysis. The proposed mechanistic link between HUS1 gene loss and increased mutation rate (C57, C89) is speculative but reasonable given the known role of HUS1 in genome stability (supported by C88). However, C89 appropriately uses cautious language ('could possibly be related').

results.result: Most evolved hybrid clones showed slight SNP density decrease (except 1D12-3), with clone-specific patterns of new variants. Chromosome-level SNP patterns remained similar over time, with some chromosomes (5, 11, 24, 37) showing consistently higher density. Novel SNPs were enriched for non-synonymous mutations in surface protein-coding genes, suggesting these regions mutate faster than the rest of the genome.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C67 are supported by comprehensive SNP analysis across all evolved clones with chromosome-level resolution. The enrichment of mutations in surface protein genes is consistently observed in both parental (C65) and hybrid (C66) evolved clones. The inference that surface molecule-coding regions mutate faster (C67) is well-supported by the data, though the mechanism remains to be determined.

results.result: Initial hybrid clones were tetraploid, formed by fusion of diploid parental genomes (evidenced by inheritance of SNPs from both parents), with gradual genome erosion over time. This confirms parasexual hybridization in T. cruzi, resembling Candida albicans parasexual cycle, distinct from the meiosis-like process in T. brucei and Leishmania.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 synthesize multiple lines of evidence (ploidy, SNP inheritance, erosion patterns) to support parasexual hybridization. The comparison to C. albicans (C72) and contrast with T. brucei/Leishmania (C73) are appropriately supported by citations. However, C69 acknowledges that 'more complex pathways cannot be ruled out in the absence of direct observational evidence,' appropriately noting the limitation of inferring mechanism from genomic data alone.

results.result: T. cruzi genomes are highly responsive to environmental conditions, showing dynamic aneuploidy and CNV. Surface genes were eroded while metabolism/cell division genes expanded during culture adaptation. Aneuploidy (particularly chr 37 in all clones) appears to provide fitness benefits in culture and is rapidly reversed when no longer beneficial.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C81 are supported by the observed CNV and CCNV changes during culture growth. The interpretation of environmental responsiveness is well-supported by the data. Claims about aneuploidy in natural populations (C76) and its role in adaptation (C77, C81) are appropriately supported by citations. The inference about fitness benefits (C80) is reasonable given the consistent observation across all clones.

results.result: Hybridization increased genetic sequence diversity through both new mutations and likely recombination. P2 showed higher mutation rate than P1 after 800 generations. TcI strains have more efficient mismatch repair than other DTUs, and HUS1 is required for genome stability in Leishmania.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C86 are supported by SNP analysis data. The inference of recombination (C84) is reasonable but not directly demonstrated. Claims about TcI mismatch repair efficiency (C87) and HUS1 function (C88) are appropriately supported by citations to prior work, providing context for interpreting the observed mutation rate differences.

results.result: Culture growth led to reduction in genetic variants in most evolved clones, likely due to loss of heterozygosity and genome erosion. No bias in loss of specific parental chromosomes was observed, suggesting recombination. Hybrids would likely stabilize at diploidy with chromosomes from both parents and higher polymorphism than parents, similar to natural TcV/TcVI hybrids.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C92 are supported by SNP density analysis over time. However, the prediction that hybrids will stabilize at diploidy (C93) is speculative, appropriately qualified with 'it is likely.' The comparison to natural hybrids (C94-C95) is supported by citations but the claim that in vitro hybrid formation is 'highly similar' to natural hybrid formation (C95) is an inference that extends beyond the direct evidence, as the natural hybridization process was not directly observed.

results.result: Surface protein-coding genes show higher genetic diversity and more rapid evolution than other genomic regions. Distinct genomic signatures and amino acid substitutions accumulated in both parental and hybrid clones after relatively few generations. Higher recombination frequency in repeat-rich regions likely contributes to this pattern.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C97 are well-supported by SNP distribution and mutation rate analysis throughout the study. The inference about higher recombination in repeat-rich regions (C98) is supported by citation to prior work and is consistent with the observed patterns. The comparison to natural T. cruzi strains (C99) is appropriately supported by citation.

results.result: Natural inter-DTU hybridization between TcII and TcIII generated TcV and TcVI. Evidence for TcI/TcIV genetic exchange exists from phylogenetic incongruence. However, genetic exchange frequency appears too low to disrupt clade stability, likely due to ecological/geographical isolation and potentially high fitness costs of tetraploidy in the wild.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C102 about natural hybridization and clade stability are appropriately supported by citations. However, the explanations for clade robustness (C103) and fitness costs of tetraploidy (C104) are speculative inferences, though reasonable. C103 and C104 appropriately use cautious language ('likely promoted,' 'may also be').

results.result: In vitro T. cruzi hybrid formation occurs via parasexual mechanism, representing an important mechanism of genetic diversification. Tetraploid hybrids show progressive genome erosion shaped by environmental selective pressure. Hybrids show increased coding sequence diversity from new mutations and recombination. Repetitive gene families related to immune evasion evolve more rapidly than other genomic regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C108 appropriately summarize the major findings of the study. Each summary claim is supported by the detailed results presented earlier. The conclusions are appropriately qualified and acknowledge both demonstrated findings (parasexual mechanism, genome erosion, increased diversity) and inferences (role of selective pressure, intrinsic mechanism of variation).

results.result: Background claims establish that T. cruzi causes Chagas disease, has complex transmission cycles, displays diverse surface proteins encoded by repetitive genomic regions, and has debated reproductive modes. Natural TcV/TcVI hybrids exist, and in vitro hybrid formation has been demonstrated with non-Mendelian inheritance and elevated DNA content, suggesting parasexual mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C17 provide background context appropriately supported by citations to prior literature. These establish the scientific foundation for the current study but do not represent new findings from this work.
